https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-mo.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez described last week’s sudden influx of 50,000 migrants into the exclave of Ceuta in North Africa as an “ attack ,” but has been careful to accuse people smugglers rather than the Moroccan authorities of orchestrating it. That diplomatic position from Madrid is coming under pressure, however, from Spanish politicians from both the right and left, who argue that Rabat has questions to answer about the cross-border surge, in which 88 people died . From the moment massive numbers of people began to enter the city last Thursday, Spanish Civil Guard forces reported that Moroccan gendarmes who normally assist in securing the border had inexplicably left their posts. Advertisement Advertisement That led many to suspect that such a large flow of people could hardly be masterminded without the acquiescence of Morocco, which claims the Spanish cities of Ceuta and Melilla as occupied territories. Diplomatic speculation has also centered on whether Rabat could be flexing its muscles over Spain’s recent rapprochement with Algeria, which supports self-determination in Western Sahara — a territory claimed by Morocco. “Let’s call things by their name: Morocco is using human beings to attack our sovereignty,” said Eduardo Rubiño, lawmaker with the Sánchez-allied, left-wing Más Madrid party. Ceuta Mayor Juan Jesús Vivas from the conservative People’s Party on Monday said the situation could not be characterized as “a migration crisis” because “people have the perception that this, if not orchestrated, was encouraged or permitted” by Moroccan authorities. Vivas conceded that Madrid had to do its utmost to continue working with Rabat, but also told Spanish newspaper El País that “Morocco has shown us that it is not reliable.” Since the outset of the crisis, Spain’s Socialist-led government has prioritized smooth relations with Morocco, which will prove critical to resolving the crisis, rather than pinning the blame on Rabat. Advertisement Advertisement A spokesperson for Spain’s foreign ministry insisted “the relationship with Morocco is excellent, and coordination on migration and other issues remains very strong.” While visiting Ceuta on Friday, Sánchez characterized the crisis as “an attack, a violation of Spain’s territorial integrity,” but made no attempt to link Rabat to the operation, which he attributed to “mafias that traffic in human beings.” Instead, he described Morocco as “an ally” and thanked Rabat for its help in repatriating the people who had entered the exclave without authorization. Political liability Moroccan authorities avoided addressing the Ceuta crisis until late on Sunday evening, when Interior Ministry Spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi delivered a statement blaming the sudden influx of migrants on social media posts “which aimed to create the illusion of easy access to the European space without legal consequences.” “The Kingdom of Morocco will continue to be, as it has always been with its partners, a reliable and responsible partner, firmly committed to strengthening international cooperation and coordination in the fight against irregular migration and human trafficking,” El Khalfi said. Spanish opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who heads the center-right People’s Party, this weekend demanded a clarification of “what failed in co-operation with Morocco” and said that Spain had a right to demand that Rabat deliver on its obligations on border security. Advertisement Advertisement He said he wished Spain to “have a relationship of good neighborliness, cooperation, and mutual respect with Morocco,” but that “there are things that shouldn’t be done, and if they are, they must be met with a strong response.” Still, the People’s Party has focused its broader political strategy on the Sánchez government’s failure to anticipate the sudden influx of migrants, rather than focusing on Morocco. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska this weekend claimed the country’s National Intelligence Center, which handles both foreign and domestic intelligence and counterintelligence under the Ministry of Defense, had failed to warn Madrid of any developments on the border. But intelligence sources quoted by Spain’s Cadena Ser radio network on Monday said that in the lead-up to last week’s crisis, the interior ministry had been warned that a mass entry into Ceuta could take place at any moment. Moreover, Spanish media reported that in July the ministry’s own Office for Refugees and Asylum warned that the growing number of migrants swimming to Ceuta could soon overwhelm the exclave. “Sánchez and his government lie — as they always do,” People’s Party spokesperson Ester Muñoz said . “The government was warned by its intelligence services and did nothing.” Brussels brawl Madrid’s inability to anticipate the crisis will be under scrutiny at an emergency meeting of the EU’s ambassadors on Monday, and at a separate extraordinary summit of the bloc’s interior ministers scheduled for Tuesday. Advertisement Advertisement Over the past five days, a plethora of EU leaders and far-right parties have slammed Spain for losing control of one of the bloc’s external borders and effectively bringing the Ceuta crisis upon itself by moving to grant legal status to 1.2 million unauthorized migrants . In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, 22 of the bloc’s leaders on Saturday called for EU-level oversight on national policies “that can serve as pull factors.” Ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU ambassadors, Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares pushed back against Madrid’s critics in other European capitals and said his country would “demand solidarity from all the States of the European Union.” “Spain currently has the lowest number of irregular entries on the Mediterranean route,” Albares said during an interview on Spanish state broadcaster TVE. Rather than question Madrid’s efforts, he insisted that the EU’s role was to support and assist Spain in the defense of “the only two European and Spanish cities that share a land border with Africa.” At the same time that he chided critical member countries for their attitude, Spain’s foreign minister praised Rabat for its help in resolving the crisis. “From the very beginning, Morocco offered its cooperation to try to prevent this flow of people and, above all, to ensure their immediate return, as is happening,” he said. “The vast majority of those who entered are already back in Morocco, and Morocco continues to offer this cooperation so that every last person who entered Ceuta returns to Morocco.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/16/magy.text: Menü Kereső Buszbaleset: Magyar Péter és Karol Nawrocki is részvétét fejezte ki a halálos áldozatok családtagjainak Belföld Barnóczki Brigitta Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Pósfai Gábor belügyminiszter is részvétet nyilvánított az áldozatok családjainak, és azt írta a Facebookon, hogy a rendőrök és a tűzoltók nagy erőkkel vonultak a helyszínre, mellettük civil segítség is érkezett a sérült jármű mozgatásához, ő is megköszönte a munkájukat. Radoslaw Sikorski lengyel külügyminiszter jelezte, a lengyel diplomácia az ügyben kapcsolatban van a magyar hatóságokkal. A rendőrség hivatalos tájékoztatása szerint tizenketten haltak meg vasárnap hajnalban, miután egy lengyel rendszámú busz éjjel 1 óra környékén felborult az M3-as autópálya Nyíregyháza felé vezető oldalán a mezőkeresztesi lehajtó után. A Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén Vármegyei Rendőr-főkapitányság a Police.hu-n azt írta, jelenlegi adataik szerint feltehetőleg a sofőr elaludt, őt a rendőrök őrizetbe vették. A mentőszolgálat kérdéseinkre azt írta, 14 mentőegységet riasztottak a baleset helyszínére, egy embert életveszélyes, kilencet súlyos, további 37 embert pedig könnyebb sérülésekkel láttak el. A sérülteket helyszíni ellátás után a miskolci, debreceni, nyíregyházi és egri kórházakba szállítottak. A katasztrófavédelem egy videót is posztolt arról, hogy az oldalára fordult 24 tonnás buszt csörlőzéssel, darukkal emelték ki az árokból, a videót itt nézheti meg. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: 1:05 CNN reporter arrives at White House after judge rules against Trump's media ban – video Trump administration CNN and MS Now journalists denied access to White House state dinner despite court ruling Officials deny entry even after federal judge rules Trump administration must grant banned journalists access US politics live – latest updates Jeremy Barr in Washington and Robert Mackey Thu 24 Sep 2026 21.56 EDT First published on Thu 24 Sep 2026 01.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Journalists for CNN and MS Now were denied access to the White House state dinner in honor of Xi Jinping, China’s president, on Thursday evening, hours after a federal judge ruled the Trump administration must allow them in after imposing a ban last week. “About an hour before Xi’s arrival was scheduled, the White House said CNN could cover the event, but only with a photojournalist and audio technician, notably excluding the network’s editorial team consisting of a reporter and producer,” CNN reported . MS Now, another outlet banned from the White House by Trump last week for what he calls overly negative coverage of his presidency, also said its White House reporter, Laura Barrón-López, was prevented from covering Xi’s arrival for the state dinner despite applying for credentials to cover the event. When Barrón-López asked a White House staffer why she was denied access, the staffer said she should “talk to Steven”, apparently meaning White House communications director Steven Cheung, MS Now reported. Xi’s arrival for the dinner, with his wife, Peng Liyuan, was streamed live on YouTube by the White House, but none of the major US networks provided live broadcast video of the event. Earlier on Thursday, journalists for CNN, MS Now and Politico, which was also part of the ban issued last week, were finally granted access to the White House after days of being barred from the building. Earlier attempts by the journalists to enter the building had been unsuccessful, and lawyers representing the three organizations had told a judge that the White House has already “repeatedly violated” his overnight order requiring the Trump administration to return the press badges of journalists from the three news organizations. Timothy Kelly, the US district judge who appeared skeptical of arguments from lawyers representing the White House during a hearing on Wednesday, issued an early morning order forcing the administration to return access for a 14-day period. But journalists from the three affected networks reported being barred from the building, with some having their badges taken for the first time. “This morning journalists from each of CNN , MS Now, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated,” lawyers for the three news organizations wrote in a brief requesting a video or telephone conference “as soon as possible this morning”. In a legal filing on Thursday afternoon, Micah Stopperich, the White House director of press operations, said in a sworn statement that the operations team was notified at 7.10am to restore access, and that it began reinstating badges at 7.25am. She said that US Secret Service indicated that badges were re-activated as of 9.07am, and that confiscated badges were dropped off at the entry to the building just before 10am. “United States Secret Service has represented that press passes that were turned on were available for pick up at the press gate as soon as they were delivered,” she said. The badges were revoked on Saturday, after the president abruptly ordered the three outlets to be banned over “their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS”. The outlets swiftly sued over the move, which sparked widespread criticism from other news organizations and press freedom advocates. In a legal filing earlier this week, Department of Justice lawyers argued that the ban was necessary for national security reasons, and listed examples of articles that relied on non-public information. But Kelly was unswayed, and argued in his ruling that the way in the which the White House banned the organizations had likely violated due process protections for journalists – and well-established legal precedent set in two press access cases by the United States court of appeals for the District of Columbia. “Plaintiffs are also likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process,” he wrote. “The ‘general rule’ is that ‘individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the government deprives them’ of a constitutionally protected interest.” The judge said that, based on case law, before a press pass can be revoked, the White House “must promulgate rules or standards governing the conduct that would lead to such revocation. And the reporter must ‘receive fair notice not only of the conduct that would subject him to punishment, but also of the magnitude of the sanction that the White House might impose’.” DoJ defends Trump media ban: ‘Access to the White House is a privilege’ Read more The three news organizations were not given advance notice that they were in violation of any set of standards and only received formal notice – in letters sent to each news organization on Tuesday – that they “exhibited behavior in violation of the standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including by trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information”. Michael Kenneth Velchik, a justice department attorney representing the Trump White House, argued that such a process had been laid out in the letters, which informed each news organization that they had until 5pm on Friday to contest the ban. (The letters said that if the organizations did not submit such a challenge, it would become final.) But the judge said the standard mentioned in the letters was “so vague it hardly does the trick”, and concluded that even the defendants “do not dispute that plaintiffs did not receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before their hard passes were revoked”. The judge also wrote that he was “skeptical … that defendants’ interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs’ hard passes”. He cited comments from Trump about how the ban was for content-based reasons. A hearing for a preliminary injunction will be expedited to be held during the 14-day period in which the passes are returned, the judge said. Theodore J Boutrous Jr, an attorney for CNN, MS Now and Politico, praised the judge’s determination. “This is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law,” he said in a statement. “We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.” Seemingly anticipating a loss, Trump already said in a post on Truth Social earlier this week that the White House would appeal any adverse ruling. Moneycontrol World Desk October 03, 2026 / 15:08 IST Vilnius airport briefly closed after suspected drone alert, NATO fighters scrambled (File image) Vilnius International Airport in Lithuania was temporarily closed for less than an hour on Saturday after authorities detected a possible unidentified flying object approaching from the direction of Belarus, prompting NATO Baltic Air Policing fighter jets to scramble. Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre said authorities were working to determine what triggered the alert and whether the object was a drone. The alert led to the temporary closure of the airport’s controlled airspace, while Lithuanian authorities advised residents in the Vilnius region to be prepared to seek shelter if necessary. NATO aircraft assigned to monitor the Baltic airspace were also deployed to locate and identify the suspected object. The alert was lifted at around 10:37 a.m., after which normal airport operations resumed. Object not conclusively identified Initial information suggested that the object’s characteristics were consistent with an unmanned aerial vehicle. However, authorities later said it had not been conclusively identified. The object was reportedly moving at a speed lower than that normally associated with some drones, while its signal eventually disappeared from tracking systems. Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania’s National Crisis Management Centre, told public broadcaster LRT that authorities had received reports from residents who claimed to have seen a possible object moving from the Vilnius area towards Jonava. Those reports could not be confirmed by military air-defence systems. Vitkauskas said authorities could not rule out the possibility that the alert had been triggered by a flock of birds. Lithuania’s Armed Forces issued a yellow alert for a possible air threat in the Vilnius region and Ukmergė during the incident. Residents were sent mobile phone alerts advising them to identify a safe location in case the situation escalated. Previous drone alerts in Lithuania The latest incident comes after several airspace alerts in Lithuania in recent weeks.On September 13, a suspected drone alert temporarily shut Vilnius airport and prompted the deployment of a NATO fighter. Authorities later determined through visual identification that the radar contact had been a flock of birds. A more serious incident occurred on the night of September 14-15, when a drone entered Lithuanian airspace from the direction of Belarus and was shot down by Italian fighter jets assigned to NATO’s Baltic mission. Authorities later located its remains and neutralised an explosive payload. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said the aircraft had “most likely” come from Russia, although Lithuania’s investigation into the incident remained ongoing.
